theme: The covenant cut; God alone passes through, pure grace
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 15:1-21 slowly. This is one of the most important chapters in the Old Testament. The Abrahamic Covenant is formally cut here, and the way God cuts it is shocking. Pay especially close attention to verse 6, which the New Testament will quote repeatedly as the foundation of justification by faith.
settingTheScene: Abram has been called, has separated from Lot, has rescued Lot, and has refused Sodom’s wealth. Now God comes to him again with reassurance. But Abram has been thinking. He is wealthy but childless. The promise of a great nation seems further away with each passing year. So in today’s chapter, Abram does what he has not done before, he questions God. And God responds not with rebuke but with one of the most extraordinary covenant ceremonies in all of Scripture. This chapter contains the formal cutting of the Abrahamic Covenant, the seedbed of the gospel.
observation: God’s opening words are striking: “Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.” God himself is Abram’s shield and his reward.
Abram questions God for the first time: “O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless?” Faith is allowed to ask honest questions.
God takes Abram outside, points him to the stars, and tells him his offspring will be that many. The promise is sealed under the night sky.
Verse 6 is the theological climax: “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” Justification by faith is born here.
When Abram asks how he will possess the land, God responds with a covenant ceremony, animals cut in two, pieces arranged in two rows.
Abram falls into a deep sleep and great darkness, the same word used of Adam’s sleep in Genesis 2. Covenants involve a kind of death.
God reveals the future: 400 years of slavery in a foreign land, followed by exodus “with great possessions.” History is foreseen and ordered.
Then “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.” God alone walks the path of the covenant, Abram does not.
The covenant is one-sided. God binds himself to fulfill the promise, regardless of Abram’s faithfulness.
interpretation:
Genesis 15 is the chapter where the Abrahamic Covenant is formally cut, and the way God does it is one of the most remarkable scenes in the Bible. Once you understand what is happening, the gospel itself comes into focus.

The chapter begins with God reassuring Abram: “I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.” This is enormous. God is not just giving Abram things; he is giving Abram himself. The shield is God. The reward is God. Every other promise, land, descendants, blessing, is secondary to this central reality. The greatest gift God gives his people is not what he gives them; it is himself.

But Abram is troubled. Time is passing and the promised son has not come. So Abram does something significant: he asks God a hard question. “What will you give me, for I continue childless?” This is faith being honest. Faith is not pretending that the promises feel fulfilled when they do not. Faith is bringing the unfulfilled promise back to the God who made it. Abram is not faithless here; he is faith-full in the most mature way. He takes God’s promise seriously enough to ask about it.

God’s response is to take Abram outside. Imagine the moment. The patriarch and the LORD, standing under the stars of the ancient Near East, a sky with no light pollution, blazing with millions of stars. “Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them. So shall your offspring be.” It is a visual gospel. The promise is as vast as the cosmos.

And then comes verse 6, the single most important verse in the Old Testament for understanding the New Testament’s doctrine of salvation. “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” Notice three things. First, Abram believed. Faith, not works, is what God responds to. Second, God counted his faith as righteousness. The verb is the language of bookkeeping. God moves something into Abram’s account. Third, Abram did nothing to earn this. He simply believed the promise and was reckoned righteous. Romans 4 and Galatians 3 will use this verse as the foundational proof that justification has always been by faith, never by works of the law.

But the chapter is not done. Abram still wants assurance about the land. “How am I to know that I shall possess it?” God responds by establishing the covenant in the way covenants were sealed in the ancient Near East. Two parties seeking covenant would cut animals in half, arrange the pieces in two rows, and walk together between them, a vivid symbol meaning, “Let me become like these animals if I break this covenant.” It was a self-curse oath.

Abram prepares the animals as God instructs. He waits. A deep sleep falls on him. God speaks the future: 400 years of slavery in Egypt, then deliverance, then return to the land. History is being scripted from this moment forward.

And then comes the most stunning detail in the chapter. As the sun sets, “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.” The fire and the smoke represent God’s presence, the same imagery that will later mark Mount Sinai and the Tabernacle. And God alone walks between the pieces. Abram, the human partner, sleeps. Only God passes through.

The meaning is overwhelming. In every other covenant ceremony of this kind, both parties walked through. Both parties bound themselves. Both said, “Let me become like these animals if I break my word.” But here, only God walks. God binds himself unconditionally. Whatever happens to Abram or to Abram’s descendants, the covenant rests on God alone. He alone is responsible for keeping it. And if anyone is to be torn like these animals to maintain the covenant, it will be God himself.

That is exactly what will happen. Centuries later, on a hill outside Jerusalem, God in human flesh will be torn, bearing the curse of the covenant his people have broken, so that the promise to bless all nations can stand. Abram saw it in shadow. We have seen it in light.
connection: The first promise of redemption was given in Genesis 3:15, the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent. The line of promise has been preserved through Seth, Noah, Shem, and now Abram. Today the promise becomes covenant, formal, ceremonial, sealed in blood. Verse 6, “he believed the LORD, and it was counted to him as righteousness”, is the heart of the gospel that Paul will preach in Romans 4 and Galatians 3. Abram is justified by faith, not by works. And the one-sided nature of the covenant points forward to Christ, who alone passes through the pieces, bearing the curse so that the blessing might come to all nations.
application:
Today, sit with verse 6 until it lands. You are justified by faith. Not by your performance. Not by your moral track record. Not by your religious effort. By faith, by believing the God who has promised, who has acted, who has sent his Son. Abram believed and was reckoned righteous. The same is true for you. If you have believed in Christ, his righteousness is counted to you, just as Abram’s faith was counted to him. This is not a metaphor. It is the legal verdict of God over your life.

And sit with the one-sided covenant. God alone walked between the pieces because the covenant depends on him, not on you. If your faith feels weak, the covenant is still secure. If you fail, the covenant still stands. The God who bound himself to Abram has bound himself to you in Christ. Your security is not in the steadiness of your walking but in the faithfulness of his.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that your standing with him rests on his faithfulness and not yours.
Confess any striving to earn what he has already given.
Praise Christ who was torn so that you could be blessed.
